Henry Ainsworth
hen'rē ānz'wərth
n. (Henry Ainsworth, c. 1569–1622, teacher of the Ancient Church in Amsterdam, Hebraist and annotator)
English surname Ainsworth, from a Lancashire place name, Aegen's enclosure.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Henry Ainsworth left Cambridge for the Separatist cause, lived in Amsterdam at one time as a porter in a bookseller's cellar on ninepence a week, and became the teacher of the Ancient Church beside Francis Johnson. He was one of the finest Hebraists in Europe. His Annotations upon the Five Books of Moses, the Book of the Psalmes and the Song of Songs gives the Hebrew text's sense word by word with rabbinic and Targumic material weighed and judged, and his metrical Psalter was carried to Plymouth by the Pilgrims and used there for decades. He divided from Johnson in 1610 over the authority of the eldership and led out the party that held the congregation's own power. Isa 8:20 is the standard he applied to the Jewish commentators he read so closely, and Luk 24:27 the end he read the Pentateuch for.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an annotation as a remark or note on a text, and a Targum as a Chaldee paraphrase of the Old Testament.

expand to see more

ANNOTA'TION, n. A remark, note or commentary on some passage of a book, intended to illustrate its meaning.

TAR'GUM, n. A Chaldee version or paraphrase of the Old Testament.

PSALM'ODY, n. The act, practice or art of singing sacred songs.

Key Scripture

Isa 8:20 — "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them."

Luk 24:27 — "And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself."

2Ti 2:15 — "Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth."

Psa 96:3 — "Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people."

Modern Corruption

A porter on ninepence a week who wrote the best Hebrew annotations in England.

expand to see more

Ainsworth is the answer to the assumption that separation from an establishment means separation from learning. He read the rabbis, the Targums, and the Septuagint, judged them by the text, and produced annotations that scholars still consult, while living in poverty in a foreign city as a member of a hunted congregation. Isa 8:20 is the discipline that kept the apparatus in its place: “if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20), applied to Jewish and Christian commentators alike.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pairing of exact philology with a confessional aim. He did not read the Pentateuch to reconstruct its sources but to find what Luk 24:27 says is there, “in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27). His Psalter is the other half of the man: having established the sense, he put the Psalms into English metre so that a congregation of exiles could sing them, and a shipload of them did, in Plymouth, for two generations.

Usage

"“if they speak not according to this word” (Isa 8:20) — applied to every commentator."

"“in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27) — why he read Moses."

"“Declare his glory among the heathen” (Psa 96:3) — the Psalter he made to be sung."
